title: Cholera’s hidden price tag: households in Nepal and Mozambique pay a heavy economic toll - Bioengineer.org
description: Cholera’s hidden price tag: households in Nepal and Mozambique pay a heavy economic toll  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
Cholera is usually described in the language of epidemiology: an estimated 4 million cases and roughly 143,000 deaths every year, concentrated in the world’s most resource-limited settings. But a new prospective cost-of-illness study, published in BMC Public Health, shifts the lens from case counts to cash flows, asking a deceptively simple question with profound policy implications: what does a single episode of cholera actually cost, and who ends up paying for it? The answer, drawn from hundreds of consecutively enrolled patients in Nepal and Mozambique, reveals two countries where the same disease imposes strikingly different economic burdens, shaped less by biology than by the architecture of healthcare financing and service delivery.

The research was embedded within the Enhanced Cholera Control projects, known as ECHO-N in Nepal and ECHO-M in Mozambique, and led by the International Vaccine Institute with support from the Korea International Cooperation Agency. Rather than reconstructing costs retrospectively from records, the team designed a prospective cost-of-illness study, the gold standard for capturing the full economic footprint of a disease as it unfolds. In Nepal, data were collected from 38 health facilities in the Kathmandu Valley and Kailali District between 2021 and 2024. In Mozambique, the team worked in cholera treatment centers across five provinces during the epidemic period and in Nampula province during the endemic period, spanning 2023 to 2025. All eligible cholera cases meeting country-specific case definitions were consecutively enrolled, a design choice that minimizes selection bias and yields a sample representative of the true patient population presenting for care.

The analytical framework distinguished three cost categories that together define the economic burden of an illness episode. Direct medical costs cover consultations, medications, laboratory tests and hospital stays. Direct non-medical costs capture the often-overlooked expenses of simply getting treated: transportation to facilities, food for patients and caregivers, and accommodation during hospitalization. Indirect costs, the third pillar, quantify lost productivity, the wages forfeited when a patient or caregiver cannot work. Patient interviews captured all three categories, while healthcare provider costs were estimated from facility records in both countries. In Nepal, the researchers applied a hospital-specific revenue-to-cost ratio adjustment, a technical refinement that corrects for the mismatch between what facilities earn through revenue and what their services actually cost to deliver, ensuring provider-side estimates reflect true resource consumption rather than accounting artifacts.

The headline numbers tell a story of two very different epidemics. During epidemic periods, the mean cost per cholera episode was higher in Nepal, at US$113.5 with a 95 percent bootstrapped confidence interval of 93.3 to 133.7, than in Mozambique, where the mean was US$54.1 with a confidence interval of 50.8 to 57.0. Yet the pattern inverted during endemic periods: the mean cost per episode rose to US$72.5 in Mozambique, with a confidence interval of 65.0 to 80.5, while Nepal’s endemic-period mean fell to US$63.6, with a confidence interval of 48.4 to 78.7. The study analyzed 273 cases in Nepal and 252 in Mozambique, and all costs were reported in 2023 US dollars with 95 percent bootstrapped confidence intervals, a non-parametric resampling technique that avoids assumptions about the underlying cost distribution, which is typically right-skewed in cost-of-illness data.

Raw dollar comparisons, however, can mislead when the two economies differ so dramatically in what money can buy. To correct for this, the researchers adjusted the figures for purchasing power parity, converting local costs into international dollars that reflect equivalent purchasing power across countries. After this adjustment, the mean cost per episode was I$346.9 in Nepal and I$155.3 in Mozambique, meaning that once the local cost of goods and services is accounted for, a cholera episode in Nepal consumes more than twice the real resources of one in Mozambique. This PPP adjustment is critical for cross-country comparisons in health economics, because a US$113 episode in a low-income economy can represent a far heavier real burden than the same nominal sum in a wealthier one.

The most consequential finding concerns who bears the financial weight. In Mozambique, every single enrolled patient received government subsidies for cholera treatment, meaning the state absorbed the direct medical costs rather than the households. In Nepal, the picture was radically different: 89.5 percent of enrolled participants reported making out-of-pocket payments for cholera treatment during the endemic period, and out-of-pocket payments accounted for 92.6 to 96.6 percent of total direct medical costs. In practical terms, nearly every rupee spent on cholera care in Nepal came directly from the pockets of already vulnerable families, a financing pattern that health economists associate with catastrophic health expenditure and impoverishment when illness strikes households with limited savings.

The burden relative to income tells the final chapter of this economic story. The proportion of household income represented by cholera-related costs was higher in Mozambique than in Nepal and varied across income groups, meaning that for the poorest families, a single episode of watery diarrhea could consume a meaningful slice of annual earnings. This income-relative framing is essential for understanding the true distributional impact of cholera: the same absolute cost weighs far more heavily on a household living at subsistence level than on one with disposable income, and the variation across income groups signals that cholera functions as a regressive economic shock, punishing the poorest most severely.

The divergence in cost patterns between the two settings reflects differences in healthcare utilization, financing mechanisms and service delivery models rather than differences in the disease itself. Nepal’s higher epidemic-period costs likely mirror longer care pathways, more intensive facility-based treatment and the absence of subsidies, while Mozambique’s government-financed model shields patients from direct medical charges even as indirect and non-medical costs accumulate. These findings argue for context-specific financing strategies: in Nepal, expanding subsidy coverage or risk-pooling mechanisms could prevent cholera from becoming a household financial catastrophe, while in Mozambique, protecting government financing for cholera treatment remains essential to preserve the existing safety net.

Beyond financing, the economics of cholera strengthen the case for prevention. The authors emphasize that these cost estimates support consideration of preventive investments, from oral cholera vaccines to water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure, as a means of reducing the economic burden before episodes occur. When a single episode costs I$346.9 in purchasing-power-adjusted terms in Nepal, and when cholera generates millions of cases annually worldwide, the aggregate economic toll rivals the clinical one. Cost-of-illness evidence of this kind provides ministries of health and finance with the quantitative ammunition to weigh prevention against treatment, transforming cholera control from a purely public health argument into an economic one that resonates across government departments.

For a disease long measured in cases and deaths, this study adds a third metric that may prove just as persuasive to policymakers: money. By rigorously quantifying the economic burden of cholera from both patient and provider perspectives in two endemic countries, the research demonstrates that the financial footprint of cholera is substantial, unevenly distributed and deeply shaped by national financing choices. As climate change expands the geographic range of cholera and urbanization concentrates vulnerable populations, understanding what each episode costs, and who pays, will become an increasingly urgent question for global health. The answer from Nepal and Mozambique is clear: cholera is not only a clinical emergency but an economic one, and the solutions, whether subsidies in Kathmandu or sustained financing in Maputo, must be tailored to the financing architecture of each setting.

title: India and Nepal need a common front against Himalayan floods - Firstpost
description: India and Nepal need a common front against Himalayan floods  Firstpost
publisher.title: Firstpost
full_article:
Nepal’s ambitious, six-year plan to drain four high-altitude glacial lakes—Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho, and Hongu-2—is born out of sheer urgency. Following a catastrophic flood along the China-Nepal border that left more than 1,450 dead and thousands more missing, Kathmandu is scrambling to mitigate future disasters.

New Delhi cannot afford to view this as a purely domestic Nepali affair. All four targets sit on a 2020 ICIMOD-UNDP high-risk inventory within the Koshi and Gandaki basins, watersheds that feed the Koshi and Gandak rivers sweeping into Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. For India, providing immediate technical support, data sharing, and early warning systems to Nepal is proactive flood defence for its own northern plains.

The geography of transboundary disasters is unsparing. The catastrophic August deluge surged from the Lhende Khola into the Bhote Koshi, then wound through the Trishuli and Narayani rivers before crossing into India as the Gandak to join the Ganga. By the time such glacial bursts reach the lowlands, they lose their vertical momentum.

The primary threat is rarely a sudden wall of water, but rather an acute, destabilising volume surge delivered to rivers already swollen by the monsoon and hemmed in by fragile embankments.

More from Opinion

The precedent for disaster is well-established. Just two years ago, torrential rains forced Nepal to open every gate of the Koshi barrage, triggering flood alerts across 13 districts in Bihar. The 2008 Koshi embankment breach at Kusaha permanently altered the river's course, displacing over 2.3 million people in northern Bihar.

With engineering design studies slated to begin in the fiscal year ending mid-July 2027, Nepal is drawing on past successes. It lowered Tsho Rolpa by 3 meters in 2000 for the first time and replicated the feat at Imja, a decade later. Yet, engineering has its limits.

The current project addresses only four of Nepal's 21 highly dangerous glacial lakes, leaving the exact valley that failed in August completely untouched. Where engineering fails, technology must step in.

Advertisement

Advertisement

When the August collapse occurred, seismic instruments registered the shockwave as a magnitude 5.2 event. Linked to automated alerts, such data can buy downstream communities precious minutes, provided the monitoring systems are properly maintained.

However, technology requires infrastructure and upkeep. Automated monitoring stations, lake-level sensors, and satellite feeds are remarkably inexpensive when measured against the catastrophic cost of a breached levee.

Facing a $5 billion recovery bill, Nepal cannot secure its mountains alone, and India is noticeably absent from the project's current list of financial backers. This is a missed diplomatic and security opportunity. India already possesses world-class satellite arrays, meteorological assets, and a Central Water Commission that tracks these very river systems.

Sharing this existing data costs New Delhi virtually nothing. Furthermore, the broader geopolitical challenge includes Tibet, where many of the region's perilous lakes reside. Currently, critical alerts must traverse a friction-filled path from China to Nepal to India, stifled by a chronic lack of trilateral cooperation.

But the hydro-politics between New Delhi and Kathmandu carry historical baggage. The 1954 Koshi Agreement remains a point of friction in Nepal, and any unilateral Indian offer to plant equipment in Nepali mountains will be viewed with skepticism. India must shift its diplomatic approach considering these sensitivities.

New Delhi should route its cooperation through multilateral bodies like the UN Development Programme and ICIMOD, the Kathmandu-based mountain center where India holds a seat. By ensuring data flows symmetrically and leaving station ownership with Nepal, India can build trust.

Early warning cooperation is a rare geopolitical arena where one nation's gain does not equal another's loss. During the August disaster, the river gauge at Syabrubesi went offline within minutes of the glacial collapse.

A sensor's sudden silence is a loud distress signal, but only if someone downstream is listening. While lowering glacial lakes takes years, transmitting a digital warning takes seconds and costs a fraction of the infrastructure it protects.

India's major rivers begin in foreign peaks; its domestic security is hostage to what happens in those mountains and how fast that information reaches Delhi and Patna. The August flood decimated a vital border trade route on its way south. The next deluge will not pause at the border. The only remaining question is whether India chooses to hear it coming.

title: Growth, Play and Privilege Shape Preschool Thinking Skills in Nepal Study - Bioengineer.org
description: Growth, Play and Privilege Shape Preschool Thinking Skills in Nepal Study  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
In the classrooms and courtyards of early childhood development centers across Rupandehi District in southern Nepal, researchers have been quietly measuring something invisible: the building blocks of thinking itself. A new cross-sectional study of 401 preschool children aged three to five years, published in BMC Public Health, has mapped how nutrition, psychosocial stimulation, socioeconomic conditions, and family circumstances converge to shape conceptual skill development during a window of childhood that never comes again. The findings, drawn from one of the first studies in Nepal to focus specifically on conceptual skills rather than overall cognitive development, offer a striking portrait of how biology and social environment intertwine in the earliest years of learning.

Conceptual skill development is the foundation on which later learning rests. It encompasses the abilities that allow young children to classify objects, understand quantities, grasp cause and effect, follow sequences, and solve simple problems. These are not abstract academic luxuries; they are the cognitive scaffolding that supports reasoning, language, and eventual school readiness. Developmental scientists have long known that nutrition, stimulation, and family environment influence cognitive outcomes in early childhood, but evidence from low- and middle-income countries has tended to lump these abilities together with broader measures of development. The new study, conducted by Prakash Sharma of Butwal Multiple Campus, Tribhuvan University, as part of his PhD research, zooms in on this specific domain with unusual precision for the region.

The methodology was deliberately comprehensive. Children enrolled in early childhood development centers across Rupandehi District were recruited through a multistage sampling procedure, ensuring that the sample represented the district’s diverse communities rather than a single convenient cluster. Each child’s conceptual skills were assessed using the conceptual skill development component of a standardized Cognitive Development Tool designed for preschool children. Beyond the cognitive testing, the study collected anthropometric measurements, allowing the researchers to calculate height-for-age and weight-for-age z-scores, the standard indicators of chronic and acute nutritional status. Interviewer-administered structured questionnaires captured socio-demographic characteristics, the level of psychosocial stimulation children received at home, and caregivers’ nutritional practices. Observation with standardized tools rounded out the picture of each child’s daily environment.

When the data were subjected to multiple linear regression analysis, a clear hierarchy of influences emerged. The single most robust nutritional finding concerned linear growth: children with higher height-for-age z-scores, a marker of long-term nutritional adequacy, scored significantly better on conceptual skill assessments. This aligns with a substantial body of international evidence linking chronic malnutrition, or stunting, to diminished cognitive development. Height-for-age reflects not just a child’s diet in recent weeks but the cumulative nutritional history of the first years of life, a period during which the brain undergoes its most rapid architectural changes. A child who is well-nourished through this critical period appears, in this dataset, to carry a measurable cognitive advantage into the preschool years.

Psychosocial stimulation proved equally consequential. Children whose caregivers provided richer stimulation, more talking, more play, more responsive interaction, more exposure to books and learning materials, achieved higher conceptual skill scores. This finding speaks to a growing consensus in developmental science that the quantity and quality of caregiver-child interaction is not a soft variable but a hard driver of neurocognitive growth. Responsive caregiving stimulates the developing brain through language exposure, joint attention, and emotionally secure interaction, all of which are thought to support the neural circuits underlying memory, attention, and reasoning. In a district where many families face economic hardship, the finding suggests that stimulation is one of the few powerful developmental levers that costs nothing but time and attention.

The social dimension of the results is perhaps the most sobering. Children from relatively advantaged caste and ethnic groups scored higher on conceptual skill development than children from relatively disadvantaged groups, an association that persisted in the final regression model. Nepal’s caste system has historically shaped access to education, economic opportunity, healthcare, and social capital, and this study provides quantitative evidence that these structural inequalities reach into the cognitive development of preschool children. The finding is not a statement about any group’s inherent abilities; it is a measurement of how social disadvantage, operating through nutrition, stimulation, healthcare access, and family stress, becomes biologically embedded in early childhood. The author explicitly frames this as evidence for interventions that attend to caste-based disadvantage alongside nutrition and caregiving.

Two findings ran in a direction that might surprise readers. Cesarean delivery was associated with lower conceptual skill scores, and so was increasing child age within the three-to-five-year window. The cesarean association, observed in cross-sectional data, cannot establish causation; it may reflect differences in birth circumstances, maternal health, or unmeasured perinatal factors that cluster with delivery mode. The age association is equally intriguing and may reflect cohort composition, sampling patterns, or the possibility that older children in the sample came from backgrounds with fewer developmental resources. The study is careful to note that these are associations, not proven causal effects, and that cross-sectional designs cannot disentangle the direction of influence.

The analysis also demonstrated scientific restraint in an era of overclaimed findings. Associations for nutritional edema, the swelling that signals severe acute malnutrition, and for household economic ranking were unstable across different model specifications. Rather than forcing these variables into the narrative, the author explicitly declined to interpret them as independent effects. This kind of sensitivity analysis, testing whether a finding survives when the model is respecified, is exactly the practice that separates robust evidence from statistical noise. The final model explained 35.3 percent of the variance in conceptual skill development, a substantial proportion for a study of this kind, indicating that the measured nutritional, psychosocial, and social factors capture a meaningful share of what drives conceptual growth, while leaving room for unmeasured influences ranging from genetics to community environment.

The statistical rigor extended to the diagnostics. Supplementary materials include histograms of standardized residuals, normal probability plots, and scatterplots of residuals against predicted values, confirming that the regression model met its underlying assumptions. A Pearson correlation matrix among continuous variables and a sensitivity analysis with categorical predictors entered as dummy variables further tested the stability of the findings. Ethical procedures were equally thorough: the study received approval from the Nepal Health Research Council, written informed consent was obtained from all primary caregivers, permission was granted by the early childhood development centers, and verbal assent was sought from each child before assessment, with hesitant children given time until they were ready to participate willingly.

The practical implications reach far beyond Rupandehi District. The study argues for early childhood development interventions that combine three strands: nutrition improvement to support physical growth, responsive caregiving and psychosocial stimulation to feed the developing mind, and attention to caste-based social disadvantage to level the structural playing field. In a country where nearly one in three children under five is stunted, and where preschool enrollment is expanding rapidly, the message is that cognitive development is not determined by any single factor but by the convergence of biology, interaction, and social structure. For policymakers, the convergence is an opportunity: each strand is a proven target for intervention, and the evidence suggests that acting on all three together, during the narrow window before formal schooling begins, may yield the greatest returns for the next generation of Nepali children.

title: Nepal imports 2 million packs of playing cards in two months - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal imports 2 million packs of playing cards in two months  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Demand for playing cards tends to rise in Nepal during the festive season, particularly around Dashain and Tihar. The country imports cards from several countries to meet the seasonal demand. While cards are commonly used for entertainment, gambling can lead to substantial financial losses, with millions of rupees changing hands. Imports also account for a considerable outflow of money from Nepal.

In the first two months of the current fiscal year, Nepal imported playing cards worth Rs51.8 million, according to the Department of Customs. The country brought in 1,992,265 packs of cards during the period, generating Rs31.1 million in customs revenue.

During the same period last fiscal year, Nepal imported cards worth Rs90.09 million, generating Rs54.6 million in revenue.

Nepal imports playing cards from countries including China, India and the United States. In the first two months of the current fiscal year, corresponding to mid-July to mid-September, China accounted for the largest share, supplying cards worth Rs46.78 million. Imports from India were valued at Rs5.055 million, according to customs data.

In the fiscal year 2025-26, Nepal imported playing cards worth Rs420.09 million. China alone accounted for Rs387.245 million of the total, followed by India at Rs32.251 million. Imports from the United States were worth Rs436,000, while those from Japan and South Korea stood at Rs41,000 and Rs12,000, respectively. Nepal also imported cards worth Rs8,000 from Kuwait, Rs4,000 from the United Kingdom and Rs2,000 from the United Arab Emirates. Other suppliers included Australia, Canada, Taiwan, the Philippines and Saudi Arabia.

In fiscal year 2024-25, imports totalled Rs313.7 million. China supplied cards worth Rs292.149 million and India Rs21.362 million. Imports from the United States were valued at Rs214,000, those from the United Kingdom at Rs6,000 and those from Ireland at Rs2,000. Nepal also sourced cards from Hong Kong and Italy, among other countries.

In fiscal year 2023-24, Nepal imported playing cards worth Rs321.887 million. China accounted for Rs282.346 million, India Rs26.871 million, the United States Rs9.522 million and Spain Rs2.859 million, according to the department.

Imports stood at Rs212.794 million in fiscal year 2022-23, with China supplying cards worth Rs187.6 million, India Rs21.595 million and Brazil Rs3.579 million.

The department's records show that Nepal imported playing cards worth Rs215.445 million in fiscal year 2021-22, Rs286.264 million in 2020-21 and Rs235.453 million in 2019-20.

Police arrests over gambling rise during festivals

Arrests for gambling are common during Nepal's festive season, with the number of people detained on suspicion of playing gambling games tending to rise as major festivals approach. The government prohibits gambling under the law.

Section 125 of the National Penal (Code) Act, 2017, prohibits gambling and organising gambling activities. However, the law exempts games conducted with government approval and lotteries organised with the authorisation of the competent authority.

On October 17 alone, Nepal Police arrested 20 people in separate incidents across the country for allegedly gambling.

A team deployed by the Koshi Province Police Office in Biratnagar and the Pakali Area Police Office arrested five people in Itahari Sub-Metropolitan City in Sunsari district. Police seized Rs371,010 in cash and three packs of playing cards from them.

In another incident, a team from the Anarmani Area Police Office arrested six people at Omchok in Ward 5 of Arjundhara Municipality, Jhapa district. Police recovered Rs122,680 in cash and two packs of playing cards.

In Chitwan district, nine people were arrested while allegedly gambling in Bagaincha Tole, Ward 10 of Ratnanagar Municipality. Police from the Ratnanagar Tandi Area Police Office seized Rs110,255 in cash and one pack of playing cards.

Police said further investigations into the incidents were under way.

Police step up surveillance to curb gambling

Abhi Narayan Kafle, spokesperson for Nepal Police, said people sometimes lose substantial amounts of their assets while gambling in the name of festive entertainment.

During festivals, police step up security deployments, gather intelligence and use CCTV cameras and drones, alongside regular surveillance, to curb gambling, he said.

Those organising gambling sessions often place large bets, shift venues to evade detection and offer various excuses when arrested. Police, however, bring those involved within the ambit of the law, Kafle said.

Playing cards at home or among friends and family for entertainment, without betting money or other stakes, does not constitute gambling, he said.

“Importing or possessing playing cards is not illegal in itself. But action is taken when gambling is organised commercially or in an organised manner, with large sums of money at stake and millions of rupees won or lost,” Kafle said.

What penalties does gambling carry?

Under the National Penal (Code) Act, gambling refers to a game or process in which a person stakes money or other movable or immovable property, or a potential reward, with the possibility of gaining or losing it depending on chance.

The law also treats betting on the outcome of another person's gambling as gambling, even if the bettor does not participate directly in the game. Similarly, placing a side bet or chhyankhe on another person's win or loss, with the possibility of gaining or losing money or other property, falls within the legal definition.

A person convicted of gambling or organising gambling for the first time can face up to three months in prison or a fine of up to Rs30,000, according to the act.

A second offence can attract up to one year in prison and a fine of up to Rs50,000.

Those caught gambling again after serving the sentence for a second offence can face an additional three months in prison and a fine of up to Rs10,000 for each subsequent offence.

The law also provides for the confiscation of equipment used for gambling and all movable and immovable property found at the gambling venue.

CARY, N.C (WTVD) -- Nearly 400 people gathered at WakeMed Soccer Park in Cary on Sunday for a 5K race aimed at raising money for victims of catastrophic flooding and landslides in Nepal.

The event, organized by the Nepal Center of North Carolina, brought together hundreds of runners to support families affected by the disaster. Organizers said the local effort has already raised nearly $70,000 for flood relief, and the race is expected to add thousands more as recovery efforts continue.

For organizer Ashish Hara, the tragedy is personal.

"I was born in Nepal, and I came over to the States in 1988. So, I've been here a long time," Hara said.

He said one of his former classmates was among those affected by the disaster.

"During the floods, one of my classmates was an engineer in the hydro power station, and he was stuck in the tunnel. We never heard from him after that," Hara said.

The tunnel where his classmate was trapped was destroyed.

SEE ALSO | NC Nepalese community rallies after deadly Nepal-Tibet border flood

The flooding and landslides have left widespread devastation across Nepal, washing away communities and leaving families without homes, schools and access to basic necessities.

"These communities are completely washed away. There is no going back because billions of gallons of water traveled 100 kilometers, wiping everything out. People are buried under the mud," a race organizer said. "That place is not ready to build any infrastructure. It's like 10 feet of mud, and a lot of people and infrastructure are buried under it."

According to ABC News, the death toll has climbed to 1,287, with more than 5,000 people still unaccounted for.

Despite chilly conditions Sunday morning, hundreds of people participated in the event to raise both awareness and money for relief efforts. Organizers said the focus is shifting from rescue operations to rebuilding communities.

Dadin Pandey said support for disaster victims should transcend national boundaries.

"When there's something damaged or anything like that, there is no border. Humanity has no borders. No matter what language, we need to help Nepal rebuild and help the victims' families," Pandey said. "They need support, whether it's in-kind support or whatever you can donate, whatever way you can help."

The funds raised through the event will go toward helping flood victims and supporting rebuilding efforts in Nepal.

The Max Foundation shared on LinkedIn:

“A mother of 4 ranging in age from 2 to 23, Jun Maya lives in a town 2 hours away from Kathmandu, Nepal.

For more than a decade, Jun Maya and her family navigated the challenges of living with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), a rare blood disorder where the immune system attacks red blood cells, causing anemia, fatigue, and risk of blood clots.

As a result, she faced frequent blood transfusions, long journeys for specialized care, and treatment costs that led her family to sell part of their ancestral land.

In May 2026, Jun Maya gained access to treatment through our collaboration with her care team at Patan Hospital and Novartis. Two months later, her family reported fewer hospital visits and no recent blood transfusions. This marked a meaningful change in their daily lives.

This World PNH Day, we recognize Jun Maya and everyone navigating life with the condition. Her story reminds us why access to treatment and support matters for patients and the families beside them.”
